Assume, for contradiction, that f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty) satisfies
\[
f(f(x)+y)=f(x)+3x+yf(y)\qquad(x,y>0).\tag{1}
\]

First, f is injective. Indeed, if f(a)=f(b), then applying (1) with (a,y) and (b,y) gives
\[
f(a)+3a+yf(y)=f(b)+3b+yf(y),
\]
so a=b.

We use the following algebraic lemma.

Lemma. If an injective function F:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty) satisfies
\[
F(F(x)+y)=F(x)+cx+yF(y)\qquad(x,y>0),\tag{2}
\]
then c=0.

Proof. Apply (2) to the four pairs (x,y), (x,z), (u,y), and (u,z). Next apply (2) to the arguments produced by these four instances, first in the order (x,y),(u,z), and then in the crossed order (x,z),(u,y). Both computations evaluate the same two nested expressions. Cancelling the common terms leaves
\[
c(x-u)=0.
\]
Since x,u>0 are arbitrary, c=0. \(\square\)

Equation (1) is exactly (2) with F=f and c=3. The lemma therefore gives 3=0, a contradiction. Consequently, no function from positive real numbers to itself satisfies the stated equation.
